resources.string: A qualitative illustration of normal urine transport, storage, and emptying after urine has formed. Shapes, fluid levels, and timing are not to scale. This is not a model of nephron function or a guide to diagnosis.
Urine already formed in the kidneys drains through the calyces into each renal pelvis, then enters a ureter. The renal pelvis collects urine; it does not make it.
A traveling wave of smooth-muscle contraction narrows the ureter behind a small amount of urine. The urine moves toward the bladder through the more relaxed segment ahead.
The ureter passes diagonally through the bladder wall before opening inside. The wall can compress this angled segment, helping limit urine flow back toward the kidney.
Urine arrives from both ureters. The bladder expands as it stores urine while the outlet stays closed.
During emptying, the bladder muscle contracts as the outlet relaxes and opens. Together these changes let urine leave through the urethra.
Bladder wall motion during emptying (Gonzalez-Pereira et al., 2025)
